(Kashish, at his desk, the evening before the vendor call)
Avni: tmrw's call with the printing vendor, should I let them quote first?
Kashish: remember last month? they said 2 lakh first and we spent an hour arguing down to 1.7
Avni: ugh yes 😩 felt like a win at the time
Kashish: it wasn't. market rate was 1.3. their number ran the whole conversation
Avni: so what do we do
Kashish: I've pulled 4 quotes from other vendors. range is 1.2 to 1.4
Kashish: we open with 1.25 and explain why, before they say anything
Avni: and if they throw out 2 again?
Kashish: we go back to our sheet, not their number 👍
Avni: ok sending you the specs now 🙏

qa.a: The range from the 4 quotes was 1.2 to 1.4.

qa.q: Which part of Kashish's plan protects them from the vendor's first figure?
qa.a: Opening with 1.25 and a reason, backed by four real quotes, puts their own researched number on the table first and gives them a sheet to return to if the vendor says 2 again.

qa.a: The vendor would have to respond to a figure backed by other quotes, so a high opening would carry less weight and the talk would stay near the market rate.

passage: At the dairy cooperative office in a Kheda district village, the private buyer's agent arrived at noon and, before tea was even poured, said, "Thirty-two a litre, like always." Sangeeta, the secretary, sighed and began arguing for thirty-four. Santosh, the cooperative's new accountant, watched from his corner desk. Last season it had gone exactly like this: the agent spoke first, everyone fought near his number, and they settled a rupee above it. This time Santosh had spent the week calling three other buyers and checking the district rates; he had a range written on a card. He slid it across to Gopika, the chairperson. "Thirty-six to thirty-eight," she read aloud. "That's what the market says. Let's start there, not at thirty-two."

qa.q: What price did the agent name before tea was poured?
qa.a: The agent said thirty-two a litre.

qa.q: What does Santosh's week of phone calls suggest he was worried about?
qa.a: He seems worried the cooperative would again argue near the agent's number and settle just above it, so he wanted a figure grounded in the market before the talk began.

qa.q: What could the cooperative do at the start of future talks?
qa.a: They could agree their range from district rates before any meeting and state it first, so the buyer's opening number doesn't set the frame.

qa.q: How might the agent react when Gopika reads out thirty-six to thirty-eight?
qa.a: The agent may be surprised and have to argue from market rates instead of the usual thirty-two, which moves the talk in the cooperative's favour.

grounding: Shows a young male accountant noticing that the buyer's first figure always shaped the milk-price talk and preparing a researched range beforehand.

passage: In the small Seoul design studio, Jin had sat in on three client meetings this month and noticed a pattern: whoever spoke a number first owned the rest of the hour. When a café owner opened with two million won, his colleague Soo-ah had bargained hard and ended at two point four, still far below what the job deserved. So before Thursday's meeting, Jin spent an evening with past invoices and fee surveys. He wrote three figures on a sticky note: minimum, target, walk-away. At the meeting the client's new representative, Leila, began, "Our budget is around..." Jin gently cut in. "Before that, may we share how we priced it?" He slid the breakdown across the table.

qa.q: What three figures did Jin write on the sticky note?
qa.a: Jin wrote a minimum, a target and a walk-away figure.

qa.q: Why did Jin cut in before Leila could name the budget?
qa.a: He had seen that the first number spoken shaped the whole meeting, and he wanted his researched breakdown to set the frame instead of the client's budget.

qa.q: What made Jin's preparation stronger than simply bargaining harder?
qa.a: He built his range from past invoices and fee surveys, so his figures came from evidence rather than from reacting to whatever number the client said.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah feel watching Jin handle Thursday's meeting?
qa.a: Soo-ah might feel a mix of relief and regret, seeing that starting from their own numbers could have avoided the low deal in the earlier meeting.

grounding: Shows a male colleague noticing that the first figure named steers a negotiation and preparing his own researched range before the client speaks.

passage: The school's bus contract came up every March, and Moinak, the youngest teacher on the committee, had watched it happen twice. Each year the contractor walked into the staff room, said a number before anyone sat down, and the whole meeting circled around it. Last year he'd opened at ninety thousand a month, and Principal Alka had felt good about getting him to eighty. This year Moinak got ready. He called three other bus operators, looked up the fuel costs, and worked out a range: sixty-five to seventy-two. He showed Alka and the accountant, Jasleen, on Monday. "If he says ninety again, we don't bargain from ninety," he said. "We start from our numbers." On Friday the contractor said, "Ninety-five." Alka glanced at Moinak's sheet and said calmly, "Our research says sixty-eight. Let's talk from there."

qa.q: What range did Moinak work out?
qa.a: Sixty-five to seventy-two.

qa.q: Why did Principal Alka feel good about eighty last year?
qa.a: Alka felt pleased because eighty was compared with the contractor's opening ninety thousand, so it felt like a win, even though there was no research to show what was fair.

qa.q: Which choice by the committee changed the negotiation this year?
qa.a: Preparing a range from other operators' quotes and fuel costs beforehand, then answering the opening number with their own figure instead of bargaining down from it.

qa.q: How might the contractor feel when Alka replies with sixty-eight?
qa.a: He may be surprised and unsettled, since his high first figure no longer sets the terms, and he has to argue from their research instead.

grounding: A young teacher notices that the contractor's first figure shapes the bus contract talks, and prepares his own researched range.

passage:
Subject: Before Thursday's venue call
Hi Dhruv,
Quick thought before we speak to the banquet hall. You know me, I'm my father's son and I check every price. I've sat in on four venue negotiations since I joined, and I've noticed something. Whoever says a number first seems to own the rest of the meeting. In June the manager opened at 2.5 lakh, we "won" it down to 2.1, and everyone celebrated. But the two halls nearby charge about 1.6 for the same size.
So this time I've done homework. Three comparable halls, their off-season rates, and our guest numbers. My range is 1.5 to 1.75. If they open high, I'd like us to calmly say our figure and our reasons, not start bargaining from theirs.
I've attached the sheet. Tell me if you think I'm missing anything.
Thanks,
Yogesh

qa.q: What did the two halls nearby charge for the same size?
qa.a: About 1.6.

qa.q: What worries Yogesh about how the June negotiation went?
qa.a: He thinks the team only felt they had won because they compared the result with the manager's 2.5 opening, while nearby halls were much cheaper.

qa.q: What choice does Yogesh suggest for Thursday's call, and why?
qa.a: He suggests calmly stating their own researched range and reasons if the hall opens high, so the first number doesn't pull the deal towards itself.

qa.q: How might Dhruv react to this email?
qa.a: Dhruv may be a little surprised that June's "win" wasn't one, but glad to go into the call with a clear, prepared range.

grounding: A young man emails a colleague after noticing that the first number sets the talks, and proposes a range built from research.

passage: Farida, you'll laugh, but I learned negotiation by watching Sudhir lose. Three vendor meetings in a row, the supplier said a price first, and Sudhir spent the next hour arguing around that number. Never from our own costing, always from theirs. So when my turn came, I did it differently. The night before, I sat with last year's invoices and three other quotes and wrote a range on one index card: lowest fair, highest acceptable. In the meeting the supplier opened high, really high. I didn't argue with his number. I said, "Based on the market quotes, we're looking at this range," and put my card figures on the table. My manager told me later, "Pema, you're the calmest man in procurement." I wasn't calm. I just knew where my number came from.

qa.q: What did Pema write on the index card?
qa.a: A range: lowest fair and highest acceptable.

qa.q: How was Pema really feeling during the meeting?
qa.a: Pema was nervous inside, not calm, but felt steady because the range came from the invoices and quotes, not from the supplier's number.

qa.q: Why did the index card work better than Sudhir's arguing?
qa.a: It gave Pema a starting point from research, so the supplier's high opening could not become the reference for the whole talk.

qa.q: What might those three meetings have been like for Sudhir?
qa.a: Sudhir may have felt he was bargaining hard while really being pulled toward the supplier's number, which could leave him frustrated with the results.

grounding: A young man who watched a colleague argue from the supplier's number prepares his own researched range before his turn.

passage: Sabina, you're about to negotiate your first contract? Let me tell you about the day I learned about first numbers. I was twenty-four, a young man working as a junior buyer at a textile firm in Surat. My boss, Mr Kapadia, went to buy cotton from a big supplier, and I sat in. The supplier spoke first. "Ninety a kilo." Mr Kapadia had been thinking seventy. But after that, every offer circled ninety. Eighty-five. Eighty-two. They settled at eighty. I watched Mr Kapadia's face afterwards; he looked uneasy. I felt uneasy too, like I'd watched a trick. So the next time I negotiated, I prepared my own range from the market reports before the meeting. When the supplier said ninety, I said, "Our research says sixty-five to seventy-two," and worked from that. That's how Farhan stopped being pulled.

qa.a: Farhan felt uneasy, as if he had watched a trick, seeing how the supplier's first number pulled every offer toward it.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Farhan in later negotiations?

qa.q: How might Mr Kapadia have felt after settling at eighty?

"Madhav, before the vendor call, can we agree on our range?"

"Why? We'll hear what they say first."

"That's what I want to avoid. Last month with the printing firm, they said twelve lakh first, and we spent the whole call fighting down to ten. We never asked if ten was reasonable."

"Hm. We did feel good about ten."

"We felt good because twelve was in our heads. I looked up three other quotes afterwards. Seven to eight."

"Okay, Divyansh. So what now?"

"I've got the quotes for this contract. Market's around six to seven. Our top is seven and a half. We open at six, with reasons."

"And if they say ten?"

"Then I say, our research shows six to seven, here's why. We start from our number, not theirs."

"You've been thinking about this."

"Since the printing call. I hated how that felt."

"Okay. You lead."

I'm Pradeep. Manjula calls me the "numbers guy" on our team, so maybe it makes sense that I noticed this.

In salary talks for new hires last year, I watched a pattern. Whoever said a number first, that number became the centre. If the candidate said nine lakh, we'd argue around nine. If HR said six, everything circled six. The actual research about what the role was worth barely came up.

Manjula was about to hire an analyst last month. Before the call, I asked if she had her own range. She didn't. So we sat down with three salary surveys and two job postings and found the range: seven to eight and a half.

The candidate opened at ten. Manjula didn't panic. She said, "Our research puts this role at seven to eight and a half, here's why." They settled at eight.

She thanked me after. I felt quietly proud of that one.

qa.q: What range did Pradeep and Manjula find for the analyst role?
qa.a: Seven to eight and a half.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel after the hiring call?
qa.a: Pradeep felt quietly proud that the preparation helped Manjula stay steady.

qa.q: What approach did Pradeep suggest, and why did it work?
qa.a: Pradeep suggested building their own range from surveys and postings before the call, so Manjula reasoned from research rather than the candidate's number.

qa.q: How might Manjula have felt when the candidate opened at ten?
qa.a: Manjula probably felt calm and confident, since she had a researched range ready and didn't need to react to ten.

Supervisor's note, procurement team review

Tushar joined us in March. In his first two vendor meetings, I noticed he said little and took notes. Afterwards he told me something: "In both meetings, the vendor named a figure first and we spent the entire time bargaining around it."

He was right. I'd not seen it.

Before the third meeting, Tushar asked Avni in finance for past contract data and built a range himself. When the vendor opened at 40 per unit, Tushar calmly said, "Similar suppliers are charging 28 to 32. Here's the data." The vendor paused, then offered 33. We settled at 31.

What I noticed was his calm. He didn't argue harder. He argued from a different starting point.

I've asked him to run a short session for the team on preparing ranges before negotiations.

Today's vendor meeting taught me something. I'm Hemant, and I went along with Gargi to negotiate the printing contract.
The vendor spoke first. "For this volume, eight lakh." From then on, everything circled that number. Gargi countered with seven. They met at seven and a half. Everyone shook hands.
Back at the office, I checked the three quotes we'd got last year for the same work. They were between five and six lakh.
I told Gargi. She groaned. "He said eight so confidently, I just worked down from there." She wasn't careless. She's sharp. The first number just pulled everyone toward it, including me, and I said nothing in the room.
So next time I'm doing it differently. Before the meeting, I'll write our own range from research, bring the old quotes, and if they open high, I'll say our number and the reason, not just a smaller version of theirs.
